title: Platform-to-Product inference narrative
content:
Purpose
Quick internal brief that reframes Redwood as the bridge from model capability to dependable product feature. This is intended for PMs, sales enablement, and the marketing narrative team — a compact, argument-driven piece we can use for decks, hiring, and lead qualification.

Core proposition (elevator):
Redwood turns powerful open models into predictable, cost-efficient product features. We give engineering teams the runtime, controls, and observability to treat inference like any other reliable production service — not an experimental research endpoint.

Why this framing matters
- Product-first buyers don’t care about model names; they care about predictable latency, cost, and reliability at scale.
- Platform teams care about consistent APIs, governance, and rollout primitives.
- Current market messages are either model-centric (pick the best model) or operations-centric (manage clusters). Few explain how to convert model outputs into repeatable, maintainable product behaviors.

Thesis (single sentence):
The competitive moat in the next phase of LLM adoption is not raw model capability — it’s the ability to serve those models as predictable, testable, and economic product features across any infrastructure or compliance boundary.

Target audience and their unspoken job-to-be-done
- Product engineering leads: ship new LLM features without surprising latency/cost spikes.
- Platform engineers: standardize inference across teams, enforce controls and SLAs.
- Head of ML/Applied ML: maintain output quality while reducing inference overhead.

Primary promise (what we deliver)
- Predictable performance: per-route latency SLOs, fallback policies, and tiered capacity so product behavior doesn’t change with load.
- Cost transparency & levers: token-level cost visibility, suggested batching/quantization presets per workload, and intelligent routing to optimize spend.
- Unified deployment surface: same API, rollout, and observability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so product teams can move between modes without re-engineering.
- Guardrails for quality: eval-driven regressions, canary rollouts, and automatic model variant fallbacks to prevent customer-facing regressions.

Top proof points (short bullets usable on a slide)
- Customers reduce per-token inference spend by 30–60% with Redwood Optimize and caching enabled (anonymized case studies).
- Median 95th percentile latency improved by 2–4x versus unmanaged endpoints through our batching + KV cache optimizations.
- Enterprise customers use dedicated capacity + private control plane to meet SOC2/compliance requirements while retaining the same routing/rollout workflows.

Key messaging hooks (for leads, website, sales)
- "Ship LLM features, not infrastructure."
- "Same API, any deployment — move from prototype to production without surprises."
- "Control cost without sacrificing quality: built-in levers for the economics that matter."

Competitor frame and differentiation notes
- Pure cloud-hosted APIs: great for exploration but often fail when teams need predictable latency and isolation. Differentiate: offer hosted ease-of-use plus migrate paths to dedicated/private without rework.
- Self-hosted runtimes: give full control but require ops lift and lack standardized control planes. Differentiate: provide a hardened runtime plus orchestration and rollouts out-of-the-box.
- Model marketplaces: focus on access to models; we focus on turning that access into product-grade features.

Objection handling (quick lines)
- "We can self-host and save money." — Sure. But teams underestimate the cost of engineering time, regressions, and per-feature variance. Redwood amortizes operational work across customers and provides tooling that accelerates repeatable rollouts.
- "Isn’t latency just hardware?" — Hardware matters, but software primitives (continuous batching, KV cache coherence, adaptive kernel selection) and routing policies often explain the majority of real-world variance.

Example narrative for a 60s pitch
"Most teams start with a model playground and discover two things fast: performance is noisy and costs balloon as usage grows. Redwood gives you a single runtime and control plane that turns those exploratory models into reliable product features — with routing that prioritizes latency or cost, observability to find regressions early, and rollout primitives so you can launch with confidence across hosted, dedicated, or private environments."

Actionable next steps (workstream recommendations)
- Bake this narrative into the developer quickstart: a one-slide story + a checklist for moving from POC to production. (Owner: Priya)
- Create two customer-facing one-pagers: "Engineers" and "Platform Teams" that swap emphasis on SLAs vs. developer UX. (Owner: Diego)
- Run an internal A/B test for landing page hero: current headline vs. "Ship LLM features, not infrastructure." Track CTR and demo requests. (Owner: Growth)

Open questions / unresolved pieces (notes to self)
- Need a tightening of the proof points with customer names or redacted metrics (legal clearance).
- Decide if "control plane" language is too technical for some GTM audiences — prepare alternative phrasing.
- Validate the 30–60% cost reduction claim across non-GPU workloads.

References and useful links
- Confluence: PLATFORM-1245 (runtime benchmark notes)
- Jira: GO2MKT-982 (landing page test)
- GitHub PR: repo/redwood/marketing/pr/217 (copy changes)

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally concise; feel free to add customer quotes or remove technical jargon depending on target audience.
- Goal is to produce a single canonical paragraph we can use in demos, then a secondary set of bullets for sales playbooks.

Drafted by: Maya Chen — send edits in the doc comments or Slack (#go-to-market).
